**I’d pick the isolated coastal town in California** — somewhere like the Big Sur coast, Mendocino, or the Carmel Highlands. If the question is where I’d actually wake up 300 days a year, that’s the one.

The reason comes down to what "money was no object" actually buys you. It doesn’t just buy a bigger house; it lets you **delete the coast’s only real weakness**, which is distance. A helipad, a light jet, a guest wing, a private chef, a proper cellar, fiber, a string quartet flown in on a Sunday afternoon — isolation stops being isolation and becomes *privacy*. Dinner in SF or LA is 45 minutes away. Tokyo is one private-jet hop away, so I’d go for a fortnight at a time rather than for coffee. When time and cost are free, remoteness is a solvable engineering problem.

Tokyo’s downside, by contrast, isn’t solvable with a checkbook. Its magic and its tax are the same thing: fourteen million other people. They generate the 2 a.m. omakase, the six-seat bar, the electric serendipity of stepping out your door — and they also generate the light dome, the ambient hum, the low-grade alertness you don’t notice until you leave. Infinite money absolutely buys you a walled, two-acre moss garden in Roppongi with perfect silence *behind* the wall. But it can’t buy a dark sky, or air that smells of wet redwood and salt, or a horizon with no buildings on it. Those are collective goods. You can’t pay a city to dim itself.

There’s a temperament caveat: if I were still hungry — building, networking, wanting friction and collision every day — Tokyo wins easily. But "money was no object" quietly implies the hunger has already been answered. Once you’re not chasing anything, the scarce resource stops being stimulation and becomes uncurated time: cortisol dropping, weather arriving on its own schedule, a morning with no notification and no reason to be anywhere. Stimulation you can import on demand; a genuinely empty horizon you can’t.

So I wouldn’t give Tokyo up — I’d just change my relationship to it. I’d keep a small apartment near Yanaka or Nakameguro and visit for two or three weeks a year, when I want the full, undiluted hit of density. **Visiting Tokyo gives you 100% of its magic and 0% of its tax.** Living on the coast gives you the quiet every single day, and turns the city into a deliberate trip instead of background noise.

Fog off the Pacific, coffee, no one expecting me, and Shibuya sitting there whenever I want it — mostly, I wouldn't. That's the better base.

Tokyo flips that. With unlimited money you can erase its main downsides too:
